Hi Felipe,

Thanks for looking at the source and for opening the issue.

Your dummy latent variable idea matches what I see. In my own fit the residual covariances of the three ordinal endogenous outcomes appear in both psi and theta, and it is the psi block that fails: eigenvalues .407, .169 and -0.269, with residual correlations of -3.55 and -2.28. The psi diagonal is positive throughout, the smallest being .048, so nothing shows up there and post.check returns TRUE.

The original data cannot be shared. Below is a simulated example with the same structure as the model where I met this: four correlated factors on ordinal indicators, a genuine method component in the items, three single-indicator ordinal outcomes whose residual covariances sem() frees, and an equality-constrained unmeasured latent method factor orthogonal to the substantive factors, as in Podsakoff et al. (2003).

The reprex (drafted with an AI assistant, then checked and corrected):
r
# lavaan 0.7-2: post.check returns TRUE while psi is not positive definite. # The psi diagonal stays positive; the matrix fails through its off-diagonal.  library(lavaan)  set.seed(1)  n <- 500 fcor <- 0.85 # correlation among the four substantive factors gamma <- 0.55 # method component in each item e_sd <- 0.60 # noise on the outcomes  cut5 <- function(v) as.numeric(cut(v, c(-Inf, -1, -0.3, 0.3, 1, Inf),  labels = FALSE))  L <- chol(matrix(fcor, 4, 4) + diag(1 - fcor, 4)) Z <- matrix(rnorm(n * 4), n, 4) %*% L  # true method component in the data, distinct from the CMV factor fitted below m <- rnorm(n)  lam <- rep(c(.85, .80, .80), 4) d <- data.frame(matrix(NA, n, 12)) names(d) <- paste0("x", 1:12) for (j in 1:12) {  eta <- Z[, ceiling(j / 3)]  d[[j]] <- cut5(lam[j] * eta + gamma * m +  rnorm(n, sd = sqrt(max(1 - lam[j]^2 - gamma^2, .05)))) }  for (k in 1:3)  d[[paste0("y", k)]] <- cut5(0.75 * rowMeans(Z) + rnorm(n, sd = e_sd))  mod <- '  F1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3  F2 =~ x4 + x5 + x6  F3 =~ x7 + x8 + x9  F4 =~ x10 + x11 + x12   y1 + y2 + y3 ~ F1 + F2 + F3 + F4   CMV =~ a*x1 + a*x2 + a*x3 + a*x4 + a*x5 + a*x6 +  a*x7 + a*x8 + a*x9 + a*x10 + a*x11 + a*x12  CMV ~~ 1*CMV  F1 ~~ 0*CMV  F2 ~~ 0*CMV  F3 ~~ 0*CMV  F4 ~~ 0*CMV '  fit <- sem(mod, d, ordered = names(d), std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, estimator = "WLSMV")  y <- c("y1", "y2", "y3") P <- lavInspect(fit, "est")$psi  lavInspect(fit, "post.check") # TRUE eigen(P, symmetric = TRUE)$values # smallest -0.108 round(P[y, y], 3) # diagonal .187 .296 .207 round(cov2cor(P[y, y]), 3) # y1 with y3 is -1.081

On lavaan 0.7-2, R 4.6.1, Windows 11 x64 this gives post.check TRUE, psi's smallest eigenvalue -0.1083525, a psi diagonal of .187, .296 and .207, and a residual correlation between y1 and y3 of -1.081. The diagonal is positive and the matrix is improper only through the off-diagonal.

Two observations that may help locate it.

The miss looks like a band rather than a threshold. Pushing further, e_sd = .45 or gamma = .65, gives eigenvalues of -0.364 and -0.762, and post.check then correctly returns FALSE. Across seeds 1 to 8 at this setting, five give FALSE, two give TRUE with a proper psi, and one, seed 1, gives TRUE with an improper one. So the gross failures are caught and the marginal ones are not, which is the awkward way round: a residual correlation of 1.08 is just as impossible as one of 3.55 and much easier to read past. It also means the example sits close to the boundary, so if seed 1 does not reproduce for you, scanning a few seeds should find the band.

It also looks specific to the off-diagonal. Across the seeds above, every case that post.check does catch comes back through "some estimated ov variances are negative", never through the covariance matrix itself, and the same is true if I fix an impossible residual covariance by hand with y1 ~~ 5*y2. In the cases that slip through, no variance is negative and the matrix is non-positive-definite only through its off-diagonal structure.

ATB,
Adriaan

messages.subject_clean: vcov not positive definite warning in CFA with 5-point Likert-scale items using WLSMV
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am conducting a scale-development study and have a question about a recurring vcov warning in CFA using lavaan.

I fitted a 25-item, 5-factor CFA (N = 200) with 5-point Likert-scale items. I specified the items as ordered and used WLSMV:

fit <- cfa(model, data = CFA200, estimator = "WLSMV", ordered = items)

The model converged, but I consistently received the following warning:

The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov) does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest eigenvalue (= -7.746245e-18) is smaller than zero. This may be a symptom that the model is not identified.

For this 25-item model, I checked the following:
converged = TRUE
post.check = TRUE
standardized factor loadings ranged from .538 to .950
all residual variances were positive
no Heywood cases were observed
latent factor correlations ranged from .338 to .811

One of the five factors contains only two indicators, so I initially suspected that this might be related to the warning. However, after removing this factor entirely and fitting the remaining 23-item, 4-factor model, the same type of vcov warning remained, with the smallest eigenvalue again extremely close to zero (3.59e-18).

I also tested a separate candidate factor structure derived from the EFA: a 28-item, 5-factor model using the same independent CFA sample (N = 200). In this model, all five factors had at least three indicators (13, 4, 4, 4, and 3 indicators). Nevertheless, WLSMV produced the same warning:

The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov) does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest eigenvalue (= -2.443949e-17) is smaller than zero. This may be a symptom that the model is not identified.

The 28-item model also converged normally (converged = TRUE, post.check = TRUE), and the standardized factor loadings ranged from .525 to .897, with no loadings greater than 1.

As an additional diagnostic check, I fitted the original 25-item, 5-factor structure using the default ML estimator, treating the items as continuous. In this case, the vcov warning did not occur. However, when I used sem() instead of cfa() and again specified estimator = "WLSMV" and ordered = items, the same warning reappeared, with exactly the same smallest eigenvalue (-7.746245e-18).

Therefore, the warning appears repeatedly when I specify the 5-point Likert-scale items as ordered and use WLSMV, and it persists even after removing the two-indicator factor and when testing another factor structure in which all factors have at least three indicators.

I would greatly appreciate your advice on the following questions:
Given that the models converge, post.check = TRUE, no Heywood cases are observed, and the smallest eigenvalues are extremely close to zero (approximately 10^-18 to 10^-17), could these warnings reflect numerical near-singularity or numerical precision rather than substantive model non-identification?
Are there any additional diagnostics you would recommend before interpreting and reporting the WLSMV CFA results?
In the 25-item model, should the two-indicator factor be considered a separate identification concern even though removing the entire factor did not eliminate the vcov warning?

I am using lavaan version 0.7-2.

Thank you very much for your time and guidance.

messages.body_plain:
Your n = 200 for 25 ordinal items and 5 factors may be the core
issue. It may be making parameter estimates unstable and also making
the vcov estimate itself unstable. You might consider simulating a
larger sample with the same summary statistics as your n = 200 sample
and seeing whether the message persists.
     With only n = 200 and 5 response categories per item, your
responses will be distributed across 5 x 5 grids for each pair of
observed variables. It may be that there are pairs of variables with a
large number of empty cells--or maybe a few observed variables with
"wild card" observations that don't conform to the overall pattern..
That would certainly contribute to instability. Looking at 2 x 2
crosstabs will be tedious, but it is always a good idea to look at the
data.
     To better understand where the issue lies, I was going to suggest
that you request the correlation matrix of the parameter estimates,
but I don't see such a keyword in the R manual. (You
could--tediously--request the vcov and standardize it yourself.) You
would be looking for correlations *very* close to +/-1, because values
beyond +/- 0.9 can occur even in stable solutions. In addition,
near-singularity can happen when no single correlation is extremely
large but a pattern of large correlations exists. Still, you may find
that teh instability revolves around what is essentially a nuisance
parameter. If you can report that to a reader or reviewer, that would
support the case that the warning is not a major concern.
     Knowing which specific parameter estimates are involved would
also help you to invoke another checking strategy--specifying various
starting values and then seeing whether the model converges to the
same solution, or deviates.

messages.body_plain:
Thank you very much for your detailed and helpful response.

Based on your suggestions, I performed two additional checks on the 28-item, 5-factor model (N = 200) that produced the same vcov warning.

First, I obtained the variance-covariance matrix of the parameter estimates (vcov) and standardized it to examine the correlations among the parameter estimates. There were five pairs with |r| > .95, and all of them involved only the first thresholds (t1). Four of these correlations were 1.000000000000000, and the remaining one was 0.999999999999999. In contrast, I found no correlations above |.95| involving factor loadings or factor covariances.

I also examined the response distributions of the items involved in these nearly perfect correlations between the first thresholds. For each of these items, only 1–2 out of 200 participants (0.5–1.0%) selected response category 1.

Second, I examined the empty cells in the 5 × 5 pairwise response tables, as you suggested. Among the 378 possible item pairs for the 28 items, 377 pairs had at least one empty cell. The mean number of empty cells per item pair was 8.35 (median = 8.5, range = 0–15).

I would like to make sure that I am interpreting these findings correctly. Would it be reasonable to view this as the situation you described in which the instability is concentrated in nuisance parameters, such as thresholds, rather than in substantive measurement-model parameters such as factor loadings or factor relationships?

Also, considering together the nearly perfect correlations among the first-threshold estimates, the sparsity of the lowest response category, and the large number of empty cells in the 5 × 5 pairwise response tables, would it be reasonable to interpret the vcov warning as possibly reflecting numerical instability associated with sparse ordinal response distributions rather than a substantive model non-identification problem?

If so, I would greatly appreciate your advice on whether these diagnostic findings provide sufficient support for considering the warning unlikely to represent a major problem, or whether further diagnostic checks would still be warranted.

Thank you again for your time and helpful guidance.

hoped for. I agree with your interpretation. I think you can complete
the case for your interpretation by collapsing the first and second

analysis produces essentially the same findings as the original--and

interpretation that you describe.

encounter the same warning) and for reviewers (who may seek to
reproduce your analysis during the review process) and editors, it
will be good to include a brief description of your diagnostic efforts
and results in a footnote explaining why you are moving past the
warning message and carrying on with your interpretation.
     The core issue, I think, is sample size. Textbooks and other
literature from the 1980s says that n = 200 is sufficient for factor
analysis. This was poor general advice, and never well-defended, but
it was popular. Today, especially with texotic estimators (like WLS
variants) in common use, and with ordinal data in  particular, we need
to think more carefully about sample size. There probably is ample
room for a paper in a good journal that updates and defends an
evidence-based approach for setting necessary sample size in CFA.
     Good luck with your research.

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I have a question regarding conducting confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) in lavaan using a correlation matrix rather than a covariance matrix.

I am aware that lavaan allows a correlation matrix to be supplied as input through the "sample.cov" argument. However, my question concerns the statistical implications of doing so.

I have a correlation matrix and would like to fit a three-factor CFA model to it. In some sources, and particularly in Rex B. Kline(2023, p. 141), it is stated that conducting CFA or structural equation modeling based on a correlation matrix requires imposing nonlinear constraints manually. The rationale seems to be related to the fact that a correlation matrix has standardized variances and therefore does not contain the original variance information.

I would therefore like to ask:

1. Is it statistically appropriate to fit a CFA model directly to a correlation matrix in lavaan by specifying it through "sample.cov"?
2. If so, does lavaan automatically handle the implications of using a correlation matrix, or are additional constraints or adjustments required?
3. What exactly does Kline mean by the statement that nonlinear constraints need to be imposed when CFA/SEM is based on a correlation matrix?
4. Are there any references, papers, or examples that discuss this issue specifically in relation to lavaan?

I would be very grateful for any clarification or references, particularly from those who have experience with CFA/SEM based on correlation matrices.

Thank you in advance for your help.
Asghar

What package did Cudeck report using? Different SEM packages use different optimization approaches. Some packages are optimized for strictly correct models while other packages are optimized assuming that models will typically have small discrepancies. If the chi-square for this model is not exactly 0, then I might expect some small differences between solutions, even though both packages relied upon "maximum likelihood" estimation. I believe that lavaan allows you to alter the precision of its optimizer--how much of a change in values from iteration to iteration amounts to a meaningful improvement. You might try changing that (no, I have never felt the need) to see whether your results come closer to those that Cudeck reported.

messages.subject: WLSMV vs. MLR for CFA/SEM with floor effects across Likert indicators — how to interpret CFI discrepancy?
messages.subject_clean: WLSMV vs. MLR for CFA/SEM with floor effects across Likert indicators — how to interpret CFI discrepancy?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm still fairly new to lavaan and would appreciate some guidance. Thanks in advance!

I'm fitting a CFA/SEM in lavaan with an 8-factor measurement model, N > 800. All indicators are ordinal Likert-type items (5-point scale, 27 indicators in total). One factor is my main outcome for now, and the other seven are exogenous predictor constructs, which might become endogenous in later re-estimations.

The structural model regresses the outcome factor on the seven predictor factors plus a few manifest covariates (age, gender, usage frequency, and some single-item covariates).

When checking the item distributions, I noticed that for about one third of my 27 ordinal items, most responses fall at the scale minimum (floor effects).

I initially ran everything with estimator = "WLSMV" and ordered = <all 27 indicators>. After discussions with colleagues, I was advised to switch to estimator = "MLR" and treat the Likert items as numeric, on the grounds that (a) WLSMV is primarily intended for ordinal endogenous variables rather than ordinal exogenous predictors, and (b) the lavaan documentation notes that ordinal categorical variables are often treated as numeric in practice.

When comparing the same measurement model under both estimators, cfi.robust came out noticeably higher under WLSMV than under MLR. I wonder whether this gap is related to the floor effects since for several items effectively only about three of the five response categories are well occupied which might make the numeric treatment under MLR less appropriate. I'd appreciate your input on the following:
Should floor effects of this severity push us back toward WLSMV despite its practical downsides?
We also plan several bootstrapped mediation models later. Is this feasible with ML and a bootstrap approach given our data situation?
Is there a standard way to report fit indices and to explain why CFI comes out differently under MLR than under WLSMV?

I'm happy to share model syntax or distribution details if useful. Thank you very much in advance!

Best regards,
Antonia

CFI is a function of two different values of chi-square: The null model, and the fitted model. If CFI changes it can be because one, or both, of those changed.

If you could tell us the four values (WLSMV, MLR) x (fitted, null) it might give some clues as to what is happening.

My *guess* is that the null chi-square is higher in the WLSMV model, because the WLMSV will give higher correlations with a floor effect.

>
> Hi Felipe,
>
> Thanks for looking at the source and for opening the issue.
>
> Your dummy latent variable idea matches what I see. In my own fit the residual covariances of the three ordinal endogenous outcomes appear in both psi and theta, and it is the psi block that fails: eigenvalues .407, .169 and -0.269, with residual correlations of -3.55 and -2.28. The psi diagonal is positive throughout, the smallest being .048, so nothing shows up there and post.check returns TRUE.
>
> The original data cannot be shared. Below is a simulated example with the same structure as the model where I met this: four correlated factors on ordinal indicators, a genuine method component in the items, three single-indicator ordinal outcomes whose residual covariances sem() frees, and an equality-constrained unmeasured latent method factor orthogonal to the substantive factors, as in Podsakoff et al. (2003).
>
> The reprex (drafted with an AI assistant, then checked and corrected):
> r
> # lavaan 0.7-2: post.check returns TRUE while psi is not positive definite. # The psi diagonal stays positive; the matrix fails through its off-diagonal.  library(lavaan)  set.seed(1)  n <- 500 fcor <- 0.85 # correlation among the four substantive factors gamma <- 0.55 # method component in each item e_sd <- 0.60 # noise on the outcomes  cut5 <- function(v) as.numeric(cut(v, c(-Inf, -1, -0.3, 0.3, 1, Inf),  labels = FALSE))  L <- chol(matrix(fcor, 4, 4) + diag(1 - fcor, 4)) Z <- matrix(rnorm(n * 4), n, 4) %*% L  # true method component in the data, distinct from the CMV factor fitted below m <- rnorm(n)  lam <- rep(c(.85, .80, .80), 4) d <- data.frame(matrix(NA, n, 12)) names(d) <- paste0("x", 1:12) for (j in 1:12) {  eta <- Z[, ceiling(j / 3)]  d[[j]] <- cut5(lam[j] * eta + gamma * m +  rnorm(n, sd = sqrt(max(1 - lam[j]^2 - gamma^2, .05)))) }  for (k in 1:3)  d[[paste0("y", k)]] <- cut5(0.75 * rowMeans(Z) + rnorm(n, sd = e_sd))  mod <- '  F1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3  F2 =~ x4 + x5 + x6  F3 =~ x7 + x8 + x9  F4 =~ x10 + x11 + x12   y1 + y2 + y3 ~ F1 + F2 + F3 + F4   CMV =~ a*x1 + a*x2 + a*x3 + a*x4 + a*x5 + a*x6 +  a*x7 + a*x8 + a*x9 + a*x10 + a*x11 + a*x12  CMV ~~ 1*CMV  F1 ~~ 0*CMV  F2 ~~ 0*CMV  F3 ~~ 0*CMV  F4 ~~ 0*CMV '  fit <- sem(mod, d, ordered = names(d), std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, estimator = "WLSMV")  y <- c("y1", "y2", "y3") P <- lavInspect(fit, "est")$psi  lavInspect(fit, "post.check") # TRUE eigen(P, symmetric = TRUE)$values # smallest -0.108 round(P[y, y], 3) # diagonal .187 .296 .207 round(cov2cor(P[y, y]), 3) # y1 with y3 is -1.081
>
> On lavaan 0.7-2, R 4.6.1, Windows 11 x64 this gives post.check TRUE, psi's smallest eigenvalue -0.1083525, a psi diagonal of .187, .296 and .207, and a residual correlation between y1 and y3 of -1.081. The diagonal is positive and the matrix is improper only through the off-diagonal.
>
> Two observations that may help locate it.
>
> The miss looks like a band rather than a threshold. Pushing further, e_sd = .45 or gamma = .65, gives eigenvalues of -0.364 and -0.762, and post.check then correctly returns FALSE. Across seeds 1 to 8 at this setting, five give FALSE, two give TRUE with a proper psi, and one, seed 1, gives TRUE with an improper one. So the gross failures are caught and the marginal ones are not, which is the awkward way round: a residual correlation of 1.08 is just as impossible as one of 3.55 and much easier to read past. It also means the example sits close to the boundary, so if seed 1 does not reproduce for you, scanning a few seeds should find the band.
>
> It also looks specific to the off-diagonal. Across the seeds above, every case that post.check does catch comes back through "some estimated ov variances are negative", never through the covariance matrix itself, and the same is true if I fix an impossible residual covariance by hand with y1 ~~ 5*y2. In the cases that slip through, no variance is negative and the matrix is non-positive-definite only through its off-diagonal structure.
